note: Compares NIST, ISO 42001 and the AI Act and adds sovereignty as a risk dimension, useful for clients with data location constraints.
title: AI Risk Governance for Advancing Digital Sovereignty in Data-Driven Systems: An Integrated Multi-Layer Framework
explain_beginner: The paper looks at how rules for artificial intelligence should also protect who controls data and systems. It compares three well-known governance approaches, then proposes a new framework with four layers, from laws down to daily operations. It groups risks into five kinds, including one for sovereignty, meaning a country or institution keeps meaningful control over its digital systems. The authors analyze the idea in healthcare, finance, and critical infrastructure. They conclude that good governance depends on all layers working together, not just one. The framework is still a theoretical proposal, not yet proven in real organizations, so it needs testing.
explain_business: For executives, this paper argues that AI governance should include control over where data and systems reside, not just compliance with standard risk rules. It compares NIST, ISO/IEC 42001, and the EU AI Act, then offers a four-layer model that connects policy, oversight, technical controls, and operations. The model treats sovereignty as a distinct risk area alongside technical, ethical, security, and systemic risks. It is analyzed in healthcare, finance, and critical infrastructure. The practical decision is whether to adopt a governance approach that is tailored to local control needs and institutional capacity. However, the framework is conceptual, so it should guide planning, not replace validation.
explain_practitioner: The authors conducted a systematic literature review and synthesized existing AI governance approaches, including NIST, ISO/IEC 42001, and the EU AI Act. They built the Integrated AI Risk Governance Framework, or IARGF, with four layers: policy and regulations, institutional oversight, technical controls, and operational execution. It organizes risks into technical, ethical, security, systemic, and sovereignty-related categories. The framework uses recursive feedback across layers and is examined in healthcare AI, financial services, and critical infrastructure. Key findings are that governance effectiveness is a system property, sovereignty is both a goal and a risk dimension, and governance must scale to context and institutional capacity. The model remains conceptual and lacks empirical validation.
